--- title: "6. The log-linear solution" --- Every asset pricing model faces the same practical obstacle. The Euler equation prices a claim by an expectation over everything that can happen next period, and next period contains another expectation, and so on forever. In this chapter we solve the recursion the first of two ways, with a log-linear approximation that turns the model into three numbers per claim. You can read the economics of the value premium off those three numbers before running any simulation. The result is a formula for how a claim's valuation responds to news about long-run growth, and a formula for the premium that comes with the response. Both formulas are in closed form, so you can see which parameter does what. ## The valuation ratio is linear in the state The state of the economy is the pair $(x_t, \sigma_t^2)$, which is expected consumption growth and its volatility. [Chapter 5](05-long-run-risks.qmd) defines both processes. The claim's log price-dividend ratio turns out to be almost exactly a linear function of the state, $$ z_t \equiv \log(P_t/D_t) = A_0 + A_1\, x_t + A_2\, \sigma_t^2 . $$ {#eq-affine} $A_1$ is the most important of the three coefficients. It measures how much the price moves when investors learn that long-run growth is one point higher. For a claim whose dividends load on expected growth with leverage $\phi$ (paper eq. 11), $$ A_1 = \frac{\phi - \tfrac{1}{\psi}}{1 - \kappa_1 \rho}, $$ {#eq-a1} where $\psi$ is the elasticity of intertemporal substitution, $\rho$ the persistence of expected growth, and $\kappa_1 = e^{\bar z}/(1 + e^{\bar z})$ a linearization constant that is close to one for realistic valuation levels. The numerator and the denominator of @eq-a1 each do one job: - The numerator says prices rise on good growth news only when cash-flow leverage exceeds the investor's willingness to substitute ($\phi > 1/\psi$). With $\psi = 1.5$, any claim with leverage above $0.67$ appreciates on good long-run news. - The denominator magnifies the numerator. With $\rho = 0.98$ monthly and $\kappa_1 \approx 0.96$ at annual valuation levels, $1 - \kappa_1\rho$ is a small number, so a modest difference in cash-flow leverage becomes a large difference in price sensitivity. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Derivation: where @eq-a1 comes from"} Start from the Campbell-Shiller approximation of the log return on the claim, $r_{t+1} = \kappa_0 + \kappa_1 z_{t+1} - z_t + \Delta d_{t+1}$, and the log Euler equation $E_t[\exp(m_{t+1} + r_{t+1})] = 1$ with the Epstein-Zin kernel of [Chapter 4](04-epstein-zin-preferences.qmd). Guess the affine form @eq-affine, substitute both into the Euler equation, and use the log-normal moment $E[e^X] = e^{E[X] + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Var}[X]}$. The Euler equation must hold state by state, so the coefficients on $x_t$ and on $\sigma_t^2$ must each vanish. The $x_t$ coefficient reads $-\tfrac{1}{\psi} + \phi + A_1(\kappa_1 \rho - 1) = 0$, which is @eq-a1. Collecting the $\sigma_t^2$ terms the same way gives $A_2$ (paper eq. 12), the response of valuations to volatility news. With $\gamma > 1$ and $\psi > 1$ the coefficient is negative, so higher uncertainty lowers prices. ::: ## The market price of each shock Substituting the solved wealth-portfolio ratio back into the pricing kernel expresses its surprises in terms of the three shocks of the economy (paper eqs. 13 and 14): $$ m_{t+1} - E_t[m_{t+1}] = -\Lambda_\eta \sigma_t \eta_{t+1} - \Lambda_\epsilon \sigma_t \epsilon_{t+1} - \Lambda_w \sigma_w w_{t+1}, $$ with market prices of risk $$ \Lambda_\eta = \gamma, \qquad \Lambda_\epsilon = \Big(\gamma - \tfrac{1}{\psi}\Big) \frac{\kappa_{c,1}\varphi_x}{1 - \kappa_{c,1}\rho}, \qquad \Lambda_w \;\text{(volatility news)} . $$ Short-run consumption news $\eta$ carries the price $\gamma$. The long-run news price $\Lambda_\epsilon$ drives the model's results. It contains the same $1/(1 - \kappa \rho)$ factor as $A_1$, and it is zero under power utility ($\gamma = 1/\psi$), so persistence risk is priced only because Epstein-Zin investors care about when uncertainty resolves. The premium on any claim is then loadings times prices (paper eq. 16), and the value-growth spread is, to first order, the spread in long-run loadings times $\Lambda_\epsilon$ (paper eq. 18). ## Hands-on: solving the equilibrium `model.solve(method="analytical")` computes every object above from the Table II calibration. No returns enter anywhere. The inputs are preferences and cash-flow dynamics only. ::: {#bf09336c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd import lrrcs as lrr from great_tables import GT KIKU_GT = dict(table_background_color="transparent", table_font_size="0.92rem", heading_title_font_size="1.05rem", heading_subtitle_font_size="0.85rem", source_notes_font_size="0.8rem", column_labels_font_weight="bold", data_row_padding="4px") model = lrr.LongRunRisksModel() res = model.solve(method="analytical") vg = res.compare("value", "growth") print(f"value-growth spread from long-run risks: {vg.premium:.2f} %") print(f"price of long-run risk Lambda_eps = {res.Lambda_eps:.2f}") claims = list(res.claims) premia = pd.DataFrame({ "claim": claims, "A1": [res.A1[k] for k in claims], "premium": [res.long_run_premium[k] for k in claims], }) ( GT(premia) .tab_header(title="Long-run risk premia from the log-linear solution") .cols_label(claim="", A1="A1", premium="long-run premium (% per year)") .fmt_number(columns="A1", decimals=1) .fmt_number(columns="premium", decimals=2) .tab_source_note('Computed by model.solve(method="analytical") on the ' "Table II calibration.") .tab_options(**KIKU_GT) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` value-growth spread from long-run risks: 0.40 % price of long-run risk Lambda_eps = 5.95 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Read the table against @eq-a1. Growth's leverage is $\phi_G = 2.6$ and value's is $\phi_V = 6.2$, a ratio of 2.4. The price elasticities come out at 43.1 and 88.9, and the annualized long-run risk compensation doubles from growth to value. The small denominator in @eq-a1 turns the modest leverage gap into the larger elasticity gap. Compute the linearization constant once by hand, because a wrong $\kappa_1$ corrupts every downstream number without any error message. An earlier draft of the site printed 56.3 for the market's $A_1$, and the arithmetic below shows why the correct value is 37.5: ::: {#8ee5adc2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np z_bar = 3.24 # mean log P/D of the market claim (annual) kappa1 = np.exp(z_bar) / (1 + np.exp(z_bar)) phi_m, psi, rho = 2.8, 1.5, 0.98 A1_market = (phi_m - 1 / psi) / (1 - kappa1 * rho) print(f"kappa1 = {kappa1:.3f}, A1(market) = {A1_market:.1f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` kappa1 = 0.962, A1(market) = 37.5 ``` ::: ::: Finally, we plot the premium as a function of leverage, which summarizes the mechanism. Each point in the figure solves the model for a claim that differs only in $\phi$: ::: {#6c179fd1 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} from plotnine import (ggplot, aes, geom_line, geom_point, geom_text, labs, theme_minimal, theme, element_blank, element_line, element_text) def long_run_premium(phi): """Solve the log-linear model for one synthetic claim of leverage phi.""" one = lrr.LongRunRisksModel( claims={"claim": lrr.ClaimParams.from_loading(float(phi))}) return one.solve(method="analytical").long_run_premium["claim"] phis = np.linspace(0.5, 7.5, 40) line_df = pd.DataFrame({ "phi": phis, "premium": [long_run_premium(p) for p in phis], }) marks = [] for name, phi, dy in (("growth", 2.6, -0.45), ("market", 2.8, 0.45), ("value", 6.2, -0.45)): y = long_run_premium(phi) marks.append({"name": name, "phi": phi, "premium": y, "label_x": phi + 0.1, "label_y": y + dy}) pts = pd.DataFrame(marks) p = ( ggplot(line_df, aes("phi", "premium")) + geom_line(color="#7a1f1f", size=1.1) + geom_point(pts, aes("phi", "premium"), color="#1b1714", size=2) + geom_text(pts, aes(x="label_x", y="label_y", label="name"), color="#1b1714", size=9, ha="left") + labs(x="long-run leverage φ", y="long-run premium (% per year)") + theme_minimal(base_size=11) + theme(figure_size=(6.5, 3.4), text=element_text(color="#2d2926"), panel_grid_minor=element_blank(), panel_grid_major=element_line(color="#e2d6c4", size=0.4), axis_line=element_line(color="#1b1714", size=0.5), legend_title=element_blank(), legend_position="top") ) p.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Annualized long-run risk premium against cash-flow leverage φ. The relation steepens because A₁ and the loading both grow with φ; growth (2.6), market (2.8) and value (6.2) are marked.](06-log-linear-solution_files/figure-ipynb/cell-4-output-1.png){width=312 height=163} ::: ::: ::: {.firewall} **Where each number comes from.** Every table and figure in this chapter is computed by the code cells above, which run when the site is built: `LongRunRisksModel().solve(method="analytical")` on the Table II calibration, and the same solve on one synthetic claim per point of the figure. Download the chapter as a notebook (top of the page) to rerun everything. ::: ## Takeaways - A claim's valuation is close to a linear function of the two state variables, and the slope on expected growth is $A_1 = (\phi - 1/\psi)/(1 - \kappa_1\rho)$. - Persistence magnifies leverage. With $\rho$ near one, small leverage differences become large differences in price sensitivity and a large spread in premia. - Long-run risk is priced only under Epstein-Zin preferences, because the price $\Lambda_\epsilon$ vanishes under power utility. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Recall"} Answer from memory before opening. 1. Write the valuation slope on expected growth, $A_1$, from memory. 2. Persistence is near one. What does that do to small differences in leverage? 3. Under which preferences does the price of long-run risk vanish? **Answers.** 1. $A_1 = (\phi - 1/\psi)/(1 - \kappa_1 \rho)$. 2. It magnifies them into large differences in price sensitivity and a large spread in premia. 3. Power utility: $\Lambda_\epsilon$ is zero there, which is why the Epstein-Zin separation is essential. ::: ## Exercises 1. Recompute $A_1$ for the value claim with $\rho = 0.95$ instead of $0.98$ (keep everything else at Table II). How much of the elasticity survives? Relate your answer to the robustness grid in [Chapter 10](10-value-premium-resolved.qmd). 2. Set $\psi = 0.9$ and recompute the market's $A_1$. What happens to the sign, and what does the sign change mean economically for how prices react to good news about growth? 3. Use `lrr.ClaimParams.from_loading` to find the leverage $\phi$ at which a claim's long-run premium equals zero. Why is it $1/\psi$ and not 0? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"} ::: {#dcbee9d2 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Exercise 1: value elasticity at rho = 0.95 res95 = model.replace(rho=0.95).solve(method="analytical") print(f"A1 value, rho = 0.98: {res.A1['value']:.1f}") print(f"A1 value, rho = 0.95: {res95.A1['value']:.1f}") # Exercise 2: market elasticity at psi = 0.9 res09 = model.replace(psi=0.9).solve(method="analytical") print(f"A1 market, psi = 1.5: {res.A1['market']:.1f}") print(f"A1 market, psi = 0.9: {res09.A1['market']:.1f}") # Exercise 3: the zero-premium loading for phi_v in (0.5, 1/1.5, 0.8): one = lrr.LongRunRisksModel( claims={"claim": lrr.ClaimParams.from_loading(phi_v)} ).solve(method="analytical") print(f"phi = {phi_v:.3f}: A1 = {one.A1['claim']:7.2f} " f"long-run premium = {one.long_run_premium['claim']:+.3f} %/yr") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` A1 value, rho = 0.98: 88.9 A1 value, rho = 0.95: 60.8 A1 market, psi = 1.5: 37.5 A1 market, psi = 0.9: 29.7 phi = 0.500: A1 = -3.04 long-run premium = -0.027 %/yr phi = 0.667: A1 = 0.00 long-run premium = +0.000 %/yr phi = 0.800: A1 = 2.43 long-run premium = +0.022 %/yr ``` ::: ::: About two thirds of the elasticity survives the drop in persistence, and the robustness grid of Chapter 10 shows the spread shrinking with rho for the same reason. The market elasticity stays positive at psi = 0.9 but shrinks, because the numerator phi - 1/psi narrows. The premium crosses zero between phi = 0.5 and phi = 0.8, at the household's 1/psi. A claim whose cash flows grow with expected consumption exactly as the household's own consumption does is riskless in the long run, so it earns no long-run compensation. A claim below the threshold is a hedge and earns a discount. ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Where to go next"} The canonical treatment of this chapter's topic is Campbell and Shiller (1988), on the log-linear return ([references](../reference/references.qmd)).
